issues.legal_issue: The acquittal of some alleged participants does not, by itself, discredit the prosecution evidence against the remaining accused or require their acquittal.
material_facts: The appellants were convicted after a trial in which four co-accused were acquitted, and the convictions were challenged on the ground that witnesses had attributed participation to both the convicted and acquitted accused.
The acquittals rested on differing doubts, including inconsistencies with medical evidence, omissions about how weapons were used, and suspicious or delayed recoveries.
Two neighbours independently witnessed the occurrence, and the prosecution case against the convicted accused was otherwise supported by evidence concerning the occurrence and its scene.
issues.conclusion: The acquittals of the four co-accused did not undermine the prosecution case as a whole; the maxim falsus in uno falsus in omnibus did not apply, and the convictions could stand.
issues.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno falsus in omnibus is not applied mechanically. Doubt about particular participants does not necessarily discredit evidence against others; the court must assess the evidence and circumstances as a whole. The Court relied on the independent eyewitness evidence and the particular reasons for the co-accused’s acquittals.

predicates.appeal_from_convictions_after_some_acqui: The proceeding is an appeal against convictions entered after some accused in the same case were acquitted.
predicates.independent_witnesses_support_the_occurr: Witnesses independent of the complainant group gave evidence supporting the account of the occurrence.
predicates.other_corroborating_circumstances_suppor: Circumstances concerning the occurrence or its scene supported the prosecution account.
predicates.doubts_are_specific_to_some_participants: The reasons for doubt about acquitted accused concern their individual roles or evidence particular to them.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows convictions and acquittals in the same case, and the prosecution account has independent or circumstantial support while doubts concern particular participants, the other participants’ convictions may stand.

issues.legal_issue: A possible acquittal of an alleged exhorter does not necessarily make witnesses who described that person’s participation unreliable as to the other accused.
material_facts: One acquitted accused was said to have exhorted the deceased, caught his hair, and taken away a rifle after the occurrence.
The trial court regarded these allegations as possible overstatement and was not satisfied of that accused’s criminality, while other evidence supported the account against the appellants.
The Supreme Court considered exhortation in the context of the facts and circumstances rather than treating it as inherently fabricated.
issues.conclusion: The trial court could reasonably acquit the alleged exhorter on a cautious assessment without thereby requiring the witnesses to be treated as liars about the other accused.
issues.legal_principle: Exhortation is not necessarily padding or overstatement and must be evaluated in the facts and circumstances of each case. A possible, cautious view that an alleged exhorter’s participation is not proved does not, by itself, discredit witness testimony about other participants. The Court referred to Jainul Haque v. State of Bihar, AIR 1974 SC 45.

predicates.appeal_from_convictions_after_some_acqui: The proceeding is an appeal against convictions entered after some accused in the same case were acquitted.
predicates.testimony_attributes_exhortation_to_an_a: Witnesses say that a person who was acquitted exhorted or encouraged an attack.
predicates.evidence_supports_the_other_participants: Evidence apart from the disputed allegation supports the account of the other participants’ involvement.

issues.definition: If witnesses attribute exhortation to an acquitted participant but other evidence supports the remaining participants, that acquittal does not automatically discredit the witnesses.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution may establish that injuries to persons on the accused side were accidental where its account is consistently stated and supported by the circumstances.
material_facts: The prosecution said that injuries to an accused and another person on the accused side resulted accidentally from the accused group’s own actions.
The first information report stated this explanation, and the eyewitnesses consistently supported it.
The occurrence took place in the complainant party’s courtyard in the morning while its members were occupied with daily chores.
The complainant party’s licensed weapons were not shown to have been used, and the evidence did not indicate that the party had anticipated an assault.
issues.conclusion: The Court accepted that the injuries on the accused side were accidental in the manner described by the prosecution and rejected the contention that the prosecution had concealed its own role.
issues.legal_principle: Whether injuries to the accused side have been adequately explained depends on the evidence and surrounding circumstances. Consistent eyewitness accounts, a prompt account of the injuries, and circumstances making an anticipated or armed response unlikely can support the prosecution’s explanation.

predicates.appeal_from_convictions: The proceeding is an appeal against criminal convictions.
predicates.prosecution_gives_an_account_of_accused_: The prosecution states how injuries to persons on the accused side occurred.
predicates.eyewitnesses_consistently_support_that_a: Eyewitnesses give a consistent account supporting the prosecution’s explanation of those injuries.
predicates.circumstances_support_accidental_injurie: The surrounding circumstances support the possibility that the injuries occurred accidentally rather than through an undisclosed attack by the complainant side.

issues.definition: In an appeal against convictions, a consistent prosecution account of injuries on the accused side may be accepted when the surrounding circumstances support that account.
